Normal compression always trades punch for consistency. Push a vocal or drum bus too hard directly on the track and transients collapse before the groove ever breathes.

**Parallel compression** solves that cleanly: duplicate the signal onto an aux track, smash it relentlessly with a fast compressor, and slide that crushed energy quietly underneath the untouched original.

> Keep the original transients wide open. Let the crushed bus carry the weight and attitude underneath.

## Dialing In the UAD 1176 Crush Bus

An `1176` (`Rev A` Bluestripe or `LN Rev E` from the UAD 1176 collection) excels on parallel buses because its fast response pumps massive excitement back between hits:

* **Vocals (All Buttons In):** Slam the ratio into `100:1` (**All Buttons In** / British mode), fast release, and slow to medium attack so the needle taps `20 dB` (the end of the meter) on phrase openings without staying stuck there. Blending a touch of this pins lead vocals right to the front of dense mixes.
* **Drums:** Start at `8:1` or higher pushing `7 to 10+ dB` of lively needle bounce across the whole kit. Roll off excess sub rumble on the crush track if low end builds up.
* **Bass:** Try `4:1 to 8:1` for `5 to 10 dB` of grit, or swap the compressor for parallel distortion filtered to `800 Hz to 2 kHz` so bass cuts through small speakers.

![Comparison showing reverb sends adjusting send level versus parallel compression locking send at 0 dB](writings/media/20261127-075000-parallel-routing-schematic.png)

## Lock the Send at 0 dB (Flip the Reverb Rule)

Most engineers mess up parallel routing on day one because they treat it like a reverb send.

On reverb or delay sends, you leave the aux fader at `0 dB` and turn up the send knob. On parallel compression, **do the exact opposite**: set the send to **0 dB and never touch it again**, dial in your heavy compression, and blend using the **parallel aux fader**. Changing the send changes how hard you drive the compressor threshold and undoes your entire sound. Route your main bus and crush aux together into one combined bus so a single fader still controls total vocal or drum level.

## Why Rhythm Decides What Shares a Bus

Unlike reverb, you cannot throw unrelated instruments into the same parallel compressor:

1. **Separate Different Rhythms:** Never send drums and vocals into one crush track, and don’t mix lead vocals with rhythmically different backing vocals on the same compressor. Whenever one part hits hard, it ducks the other out of the groove.
2. **Glue Matching Rhythms Together:** Send every piece of the drum kit together to one drum crush aux, and group unison lead vocal doubles and stacked harmonies singing the exact same rhythm onto one shared vocal crush bus so they lock together as a single performance.
